text:
This chapter answers the question "What is jackfruit?" by describing the plant in general, practical terms rather than strict botanical classification. It explains that jackfruit is a fruit tree well known to rural households, most often grown as a dooryard/homestead tree rather than in large commercial monoculture blocks, and that many households value it because nearly every part of the tree has a use: the ripe fruit flesh is eaten fresh, the unripe fruit is cooked as a vegetable, the seeds are boiled or roasted and eaten, the wood is used for construction and furniture (and reportedly for making musical instruments), the leaves are used as livestock (goat) fodder, and the latex/sap has traditional uses.

The chapter lists several practical points used to judge or characterize a jackfruit tree and its fruit for readers unfamiliar with the crop, including: (1) the tree is long-lived and can continue bearing fruit for many decades once established; (2) a single well-managed mature tree can bear a large number of fruits per year, with the source giving illustrative figures of trees bearing roughly 200 fruit per year, individual fruits weighing on the order of 25–50 pounds (the text also converts to local units), and describing recorded cases of exceptionally productive named trees; (3) fruit ripening and quality can vary considerably tree to tree and even fruit to fruit on the same tree, so growers are advised to evaluate individual trees' bearing history before propagating from them; (4) the fruit takes several months to develop from flower to ripe fruit, and timing/spacing of harvest is discussed as a way to keep fruit supply spread through the year; and (5) home consumption and market sale are both discussed as common outlets for the fruit, with observations that fruit sold whole versus fruit sold as prepared/cleaned flesh command different prices.

A diagram of the fruit in cross-section on page 6 shows the internal structure of the fruit: the outer rind, the central core, and the individual flesh-covered seed segments ("bulbs") arranged around the core, illustrating why the fruit produces such a large number of individually wrapped, sweet flesh segments per fruit.
